A “review fix cluster” is not the review itself, and it is not triage. It is a batch of code changes created from already-imported review findings.

`auto/review-ai_generated_debt` means:
- a review already happened earlier,
- that review produced findings in the `ai_generated_debt` dimension,
- those findings were grouped into an execution batch,
- and that batch is now in the plan as work to fix.

So the lifecycle is:

1. `review` produces subjective findings
2. `triage` turns those findings into an ordered plan
3. execution works through clusters like `auto/review-ai_generated_debt`

What happened here is likely this:
- There was already an active plan with open execution work.
- A later scan/review created a new triage requirement.
- `desloppify` did not insert that new triage into the visible working queue immediately.
- Instead it marked `TRIAGE PENDING` and deferred it until the current objective queue is cleared.

- visible execution clusters such as `auto/review-ai_generated_debt`
- but no active triage step at the top
- plus the banner: `TRIAGE PENDING — queued and will activate after objective work is complete`

So yes, conceptually triage belongs after reviews in the cycle. In this repo’s current tool state, the new triage step is deferred because there is already an existing execution queue in progress. The cluster you called out is evidence of an earlier review/triage pass, not the pending one.

- The run artifact shows `observe` and `reflect` both ended as `dry_run`, then `organize` failed with `reflect_accounting_invalid(missing=33)` in [run_summary.json](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/.desloppify/triage_runs/20260311_035106/run_summary.json#L12) and [run.log](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/.desloppify/triage_runs/20260311_035106/run.log#L9).
- In the runner, `execute_stage()` always calls `preflight_stage()` before the dry-run short-circuit in `_run_subprocess_stage()` at [orchestrator_codex_pipeline_execution.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/runner/orchestrator_codex_pipeline_execution.py#L167) and [orchestrator_codex_pipeline_execution.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/runner/orchestrator_codex_pipeline_execution.py#L403).
- The `organize` preflight reads the persisted reflect report from `plan["epic_triage_meta"]["triage_stages"]["reflect"]["report"]` and validates exact hash accounting at [orchestrator_codex_pipeline_execution.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/runner/orchestrator_codex_pipeline_execution.py#L194).
- But in `dry_run`, reflect never gets persisted; the subprocess path returns early with `"status": "dry_run"` at [orchestrator_codex_pipeline_execution.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/runner/orchestrator_codex_pipeline_execution.py#L404). So `organize` sees an empty reflect report and concludes all 33 issue hashes are missing.

So the bug is:
- `--dry-run` still advances to downstream stage preflight checks that require upstream persisted stage outputs.
- That makes a full staged dry-run internally inconsistent.

What it probably is not:
- It is probably not evidence that a real non-dry-run triage launch would fail the same way. In a real run, reflect output is recorded before organize via `_record_stage_report_if_needed()` at [orchestrator_codex_pipeline_execution.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/triage/runner/orchestrator_codex_pipeline_execution.py#L438).

So the short answer is: yes, this is a bug, specifically a dry-run pipeline bug.

The likely fixes are:
- Skip downstream preflight validation entirely when upstream stages are `dry_run`.
- Or let preflight read in-memory/prior stage output instead of only persisted plan state during dry runs.

If you want, I can patch this now.

I fixed the planner bug so focus mode now clears itself when the focused cluster is emptied by normal plan mutation.

The code change is in [lifecycle.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/operations/lifecycle.py) and [reconcile.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/reconcile.py). I added `clear_focus_if_cluster_empty()` and call it after `purge_ids()` and after scan reconciliation, so `active_cluster` is dropped when the cluster is gone or has no remaining `issue_ids`. I also added regressions in [test_skip.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/tests/plan/test_skip.py) and [test_reconcile.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/tests/plan/test_reconcile.py) to cover both “resolved the last item” and “scan/reconcile emptied the cluster” paths.

Covered now:
- `purge_ids()` paths in [lifecycle.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/operations/lifecycle.py)
- normal `resolve` flow via [living_plan.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/resolve/living_plan.py)
- `exclude` cleanup, triage synthetic-item purges, and any other caller that uses `purge_ids()`
- scan reconciliation in [reconcile.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/reconcile.py)
- auto-cluster prune already did this
- `delete_cluster()` and `merge_clusters()` already did this

Still not covered:
- `plan skip` / `--permanent` / `--false-positive` in [skip.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/operations/skip.py)
- manual `remove_from_cluster()` in [cluster.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/operations/cluster.py)

Important nuance:
- `plan skip --permanent` is the real “wontfix” workflow here.
- That path does not currently clear focus.
- It also does not remove skipped IDs from `cluster.issue_ids`, so a focused cluster can still look “present” even when all its actionable items are skipped.

So the fix I made solves:
- “cluster emptied by resolve/reconcile/exclude/prune”

It does not yet solve:
- “cluster effectively emptied by skip/wontfix/false-positive”
- “cluster manually emptied via remove-from-cluster”

If you want, I can patch those remaining paths too.

> DEVELOPER

'but scan is a cycle boundary, not part of the subjective ->
    score -> triage visibility filter' - why is it not?

> AGENT

Because the code treats `scan` as a queue-regeneration event, not as just another item to sort among existing items.

In the implementation there are two separate mechanisms:

- The lifecycle filter in [lifecycle.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/lifecycle.py) only decides which already-built items are visible from the current queue. That’s where `subjective review -> score workflow -> triage` is enforced.
- The `run scan` step is only synthesized as an empty-queue fallback in [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py). It appears when there are no active queue items left and `postflight_scan_pending(plan)` is still true.

So `scan` sits outside the visibility filter because it changes the underlying state and can create a whole new queue. The other three phases are just ordering rules over items that already exist in the queue after a scan/import.

Why it was likely designed that way:
- `scan` is mutating and expensive; it refreshes the world
- `subjective`, `score`, and `triage` are post-scan workflow phases over that refreshed world
- keeping `scan` outside the filter avoids mixing “rebuild the queue” with “choose which queue items are visible”

So the real implemented lifecycle is:

1. drain current queue
2. `workflow::run-scan`
3. rebuild queue from scan results
4. apply `subjective -> score -> triage` visibility rules

If you want, I can patch this so the lifecycle model is more explicit in the code and UI, because your interpretation is reasonable and the current separation is easy to misunderstand.

- `subjective -> score -> triage` is enforced separately in [lifecycle.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/lifecycle.py)

Mostly yes.

The important part is now structurally cleaner:
- one place decides post-flight visibility/order in [lifecycle.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/lifecycle.py)
- `run-scan` is built through the same synthetic workflow path as the other workflow items in [synthetic_workflow.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/synthetic_workflow.py)
- `next` and `plan queue` are consuming the same queue semantics instead of relying on an empty-queue special case in [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py)

That is a real improvement in robustness, not just a cosmetic fix.

The main residual risk is that `workflow::run-scan` and `workflow::deferred-disposition` are still special in one narrower sense: they are synthetic execution items that are not persisted in `queue_order`, so [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py) now has an explicit `_is_untracked_execution_workflow(...)` allowlist. That’s acceptable, but it means future workflow phases could regress if someone adds another “implicit” workflow item and forgets that hook.

So my view is:
- the lifecycle model is now sane
- the implementation is materially more robust than before
- the remaining weakness is maintainability around untracked synthetic workflow IDs, not correctness of this specific scan-phase behavior

If you want the next hardening step, I’d normalize that too: either persist all execution workflow items in `queue_order`, or centralize “implicit workflow items” as a proper registry instead of an ID allowlist.

> DEVELOPER

so it'll always do scan -> subjecteive review - get/comm score -> triage?

> AGENT

Not unconditionally, but that is now the enforced post-flight order.

What it does now is:

1. objective/pre-flight work first
2. if temporary skips exist: deferred disposition first
3. `scan`
4. post-flight non-objective review work
   this includes `subjective review`, `review`, `concerns`, and non-initial subjective reruns
5. post-flight workflow items
   typically `import-scores` / `communicate-score` / `score-checkpoint` / `create-plan`, in their workflow priority order
6. `triage`

Two important caveats:
- Initial subjective reviews still short-circuit to the front when they exist.
- The “score” phase is really “workflow items after review,” not just one single score item.

So the simplified answer is: yes, post-flight is now effectively `scan -> review -> workflow/score -> triage`, with deferred disposition able to appear before scan.

> DEVELOPER

and what's objective/pre-flight work first? Is that not the same as the other sequence?

> AGENT

No. They are different phases.

`objective/pre-flight work` means the normal execution queue of real fix work:
- mechanical issues like `smells`, `dict_keys`, `security`, `test_coverage`, `unused`, etc.
- clustered fix batches built from those issues
- basically “change code until the current planned backlog is drained”

That happens before post-flight.

The post-flight sequence is what happens after that execution work is drained:
- `scan`
- review work
- score/workflow items
- triage

So the full model is:

1. pre-flight execution work
   real fixes from the current queue
2. post-flight workflow
   `scan -> review -> score/workflow -> triage`

Why they’re separate:
- pre-flight work consumes the current known backlog
- `scan` refreshes the world and may create new review/workflow/triage work
- post-flight is about closing the loop on that cycle, not the same as the main fix queue

So when I said “objective/pre-flight work first,” I meant:
- all the actual fix tasks already in the queue
- not the post-flight lifecycle you were asking about

> DEVELOPER

But what do we not do a queue like this at the very start to? or is that just the same as the end one?   - scan
  - review work
  - score/workflow items
  - triage

> AGENT

At a true cycle start, yes, it is basically the same sequence.

Conceptually the full loop is:

1. `scan`
2. review work
3. score/workflow items
4. triage
5. execute planned fix work
6. back to `scan`

So the sequence you wrote is the cycle-entry sequence.

What I was calling “pre-flight/objective work” is the middle of an already-started cycle:
- once scan/review/score/triage have already happened, you have a planned execution queue
- that execution queue is the objective fix work
- only after that queue drains do you re-enter the same lifecycle again

So:
- at the start of a fresh cycle: yes, `scan -> review -> score/workflow -> triage`
- in the middle of a cycle: no, you do not repeat that; you execute the planned fixes first
- at the end of that execution phase: you re-enter the same sequence again

The thing that was confusing before is that `scan` was modeled as a weird fallback instead of a normal phase, so it didn’t look like one consistent cycle. Now it’s much closer to:

- cycle entry: `scan -> review -> workflow -> triage`
- cycle body: execute fixes
- cycle refresh: `scan -> review -> workflow -> triage` again

So yes: the start and end are really the same loop boundary.

> DEVELOPER

And how do we make sure the actual items don't skip in? Are they in a sequence that prevents this?

> AGENT

Yes. The queue now prevents that in two layers.

First, visibility gating in [lifecycle.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/lifecycle.py):
- if any objective issue/cluster exists, post-flight items are hidden
- once objective work is drained, only one post-flight phase is visible at a time
- the phase order is:
  `deferred disposition -> scan -> review/non-objective -> workflow -> triage`

So actual fix items cannot “skip into” post-flight, and later post-flight phases cannot jump ahead of earlier ones.

Second, workflow ordering in [constants.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/constants.py) and queue assembly in [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py):
- workflow items have a stable priority order
- `run-scan` and deferred disposition are explicitly marked as always-visible execution workflow items
- `build_execution_queue` uses the same canonical queue for `next` and `plan queue`

So the protection is:
- objective work blocks post-flight
- earlier post-flight phases block later post-flight phases
- both queue surfaces read the same gating logic

The remaining caveat is only if someone adds a new workflow phase incorrectly in the future. For the current phases, the sequence is enforced.

> DEVELOPER

is this well-engineered?

> AGENT

Yes, now it is reasonably well-engineered.

Why:
- phase ordering is centralized in [lifecycle.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/lifecycle.py) instead of being split across separate special cases
- `run-scan` now uses the same synthetic-workflow path as the other workflow items in [synthetic_workflow.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/synthetic_workflow.py)
- queue visibility for execution vs backlog is explicit in [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py)
- `next` and `plan queue` are now driven by the same queue semantics instead of a fake “queue cleared” path

So architecturally it is much better than before:
- fewer hidden exceptions
- clearer invariants
- easier to reason about phase order

What is still not perfect:
- the queue system is still fairly stateful and indirect overall
- workflow behavior still depends on a mix of persisted plan state plus synthetic items
- there are still several overlapping concepts: queue order, synthetic items, lifecycle visibility, refresh state

So my honest answer is:
- good enough and defensible
- materially improved
- not yet “beautifully minimal”

If you want the next bar-raising step, it would be to formalize the lifecycle as an explicit phase machine instead of inferring phase from item presence. That would be cleaner still, but this is already solid.

> DEVELOPER

is anything in this feedback worth considering? This was just on the plan  With that frame, the proposal makes sense and my objections mostly
   dissolve. A couple things still worth flagging:                
                                                                    
  Initial review vs post-flight review. The "review" phase covers
  both initial subjective assessment (first plan ever) and          
  post-execution re-review. That's fine as long as the phase doesn't
   need to distinguish them — and looking at the filter, it does:
  initial reviews gate everything (line 126-130), while postflight  
  reviews only appear after execution drains. The phase is "review"
  in both cases, but entry differs. Worth a note in the design that
  "review" can be entered from either a fresh start or from
  execute-drain, and the items surfaced will differ based on what's
  in the queue.

  Deferred disposition placement. It currently sits between
  execute-drain and scan (lifecycle.py:140-144). In the proposed  
  cycle, where does it go? It's logically "you have deferred items  
  from last cycle, resolve them before scanning." That's pre-scan,
  so either it's a sub-step of scan or its own micro-phase. The     
  proposal's instinct to keep it within the scan boundary seems   
  right — it just needs to gate scan start rather than being
  invisible.

  The staleness problem still applies. If phase is persisted as
  "execute" and the user manually resolves all issues outside the 
  tool, the phase won't advance until something triggers a          
  transition check. You'll want transition checks at queue-build
  time as a safety net — "if phase is execute but no execute items  
  exist, advance." That's cheap and prevents stale state without  
  falling back to full inference.

> AGENT

Yes. All three are worth incorporating.

The useful parts are:

- `review` is overloaded in a valid way.
  The phase can mean either:
  - fresh-start initial subjective assessment, or
  - post-execution non-objective review/rerun work
  That should be explicit in the design and code comments. The phase name is still fine; the surfaced items differ by queue contents.

- deferred disposition should stay inside the `scan` boundary.
  I agree with the feedback there. It should behave as “scan is next, but deferred decisions block entering it.” Not a separate top-level cycle phase.

- persisted phase needs a queue-build safety net.
  This is the most important point. Persisted phase alone is not robust enough because users can change state outside the normal happy path. The queue reader should be able to correct stale phase cheaply when the persisted phase no longer matches visible work.

That last point is especially worth keeping. The right shape is:
- persisted phase for normal transitions and debuggability
- queue-build reconciliation as a safety net, not as the primary model

So yes: I would keep the plan, but I’d explicitly document those three behaviors and make sure the implementation honors them.

```json
  "patch": "*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: /Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/docs/QUEUE_LIFECYCLE.md\n+# Queue Lifecycle\n+\n+`desloppify` now treats the queue as one explicit cycle:\n+\n+`scan -> review -> workflow -> triage -> execute -> scan`\n+\n+## Rules\n+\n+- `scan` is a first-class queue phase.\n+- `review` covers two entry paths:\n+  - initial subjective assessment after a fresh scan\n+  - post-execution non-objective review work after objective execution drains\n+- `workflow` covers post-review workflow items such as score communication,\n+  score import, and plan creation.\n+- `triage` follows workflow and exposes only triage stages.\n+- `execute` exposes only objective fix work and execution clusters.\n+\n+## Deferred Disposition\n+\n+Deferred disposition is part of the `scan` boundary, not a separate cycle\n+phase. If deferred temporary skips exist, they block the scan step until the\n+user reactivates or permanently dispositions them.\n+\n+## Persisted Phase vs Safety Net\n+\n+The current lifecycle phase is persisted in `plan.refresh_state.lifecycle_phase`\n+for debuggability and normal transitions. Queue assembly still re-resolves the\n+phase from current visible items as a safety net, so stale saved phase state\n+cannot hide the correct next step after out-of-band changes.\n*** End Patch\n"
}
```

- `35473b7` `desloppify: persist explicit queue lifecycle phases`
- `03cb325` `desloppify: keep review dimension metadata monkeypatchable`

What changed:
- Added persisted lifecycle phase state in [refresh_lifecycle.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/refresh_lifecycle.py) and threaded it through queue rendering, scan reconciliation, and review-import sync.

- Added documentation in [QUEUE_LIFECYCLE.md](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/docs/QUEUE_LIFECYCLE.md), including the two-entry `review` phase, deferred disposition as part of the `scan` boundary, and the queue-build safety net for stale persisted phase.
- Fixed the unrelated full-suite regression in [metadata.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/intelligence/review/dimensions/metadata.py) so the compatibility layer still honors monkeypatched language-specific metadata providers.

Root cause is environment skew, not current queue logic.

What happened:
- `desloppify next` was running the global console script at `/Users/user_c042661f/.pyenv/versions/3.11.11/bin/desloppify`.
- That script imports the installed `site-packages` build: `/Users/user_c042661f/.pyenv/versions/3.11.11/lib/python3.11/site-packages/desloppify/__init__.py`
- That installed build is `0.9.4`, and it still shows `auto/subjective_review` first.
- `python -m desloppify next` and `./.venv/bin/desloppify next` load the repo checkout instead, and both agree that the real next work is objective backlog:
  - `auto/smells-high_cyclomatic_complexity`
  - then `auto/security`
  - then `auto/stale_wontfix`

That’s why `review --prepare` was blocked: in the current checkout, objective backlog is still open, so review is not actually next.

There was one false lead in my earlier probing:
- plain `load_state()` was reading `.desloppify/state.json` with 7 issues
- the CLI correctly resolves `.desloppify/state-python.json` with 4317 issues
- so that direct probe was reading the wrong state file and was not authoritative

So the real answer is:
- current repo code is behaving consistently
- the stale result came from invoking the wrong installed entrypoint

Use one of these going forward:
- `python -m desloppify ...`
- `./.venv/bin/desloppify ...`

If you want the global `desloppify` command to match the repo checkout too, the fix is:

```bash
pyenv rehash
```

- The cluster/plan command surfaces like [dispatch.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/cluster/dispatch.py#L29) and some of the `next` render/flow modules are also valid cleanup targets, but they are a smaller win than the import/migration code.

Mostly hardening/compliance, not major product-security gain:

- Some of that is worth cleaning up by centralizing command resolution and using resolved executable paths, but most of it does not look like a serious vulnerability right now. The commands are mostly fixed internal tool invocations, not obviously user-controlled shell injection points.

1. `auto/smells-high_cyclomatic_complexity`

> DEVELOPER

Why do you have to rescan? Why not just mark it complete when done?

> AGENT

Because the queue item is detector-backed, not checklist-backed.

`auto/smells-high_cyclomatic_complexity` is a cluster of open scan findings. Until those underlying findings are no longer present, the cluster is still legitimately open.

So:
- code refactoring can reduce real complexity
- but the tool does not know that just because we edited files
- it only knows after the detector runs again

Marking it complete before a rescan would be dishonest unless I manually verified and resolved each underlying issue one by one with enough confidence. For a detector cluster like this, the clean source of truth is the next scan.

That said, within the current cycle we normally do not rescan mid-queue. So the practical options are:

1. keep refactoring the remaining files in this cluster, then rescan when the queue is otherwise done
2. manually resolve specific findings if we are certain they are fixed

Given your earlier instruction not to rescan until the end, I’m treating this as:
- do more of the cluster
- don’t claim it’s done yet
- rescan only when we actually hit the queue boundary

So the reason is not “I have to rescan immediately.”
It’s “I should not mark a detector cluster complete without fresh detector evidence.”

> DEVELOPER

Nah, we should always mark every thing complete, no automated scan completion

> AGENT

That’s a defensible model, and it is cleaner.

I’d frame it as:

- human completion is authoritative
- scan is only a reopen/corroboration mechanism
- detectors should never auto-close work just because a rescan no longer sees it
- clusters close when their member findings are manually resolved, not when scan happens

Why this is better:
- it makes workflow explicit and auditable
- it avoids “maybe fixed” state being silently inferred by tooling
- it keeps queue semantics consistent across subjective and mechanical work
- it removes the awkward dependency on rescans to get credit for finished work

The main tradeoff:
- users can falsely mark things done
- but that is already an attestation/integrity problem, not really a queue-model problem

So I think the right rule is:
1. fix code
2. `plan resolve` the exact findings or cluster
3. later scan may reopen findings if they still exist or reappeared

That is better than using scan as the thing that completes work.

If you want, I can make a concrete plan to change `desloppify` to that model next.

Implemented the manual-authoritative completion model.

Scans no longer silently complete open queued work. The main behavior change is in [merge_issues.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_state/merge_issues.py): disappeared open issues now stay `open`, while already-manual `fixed`/`wontfix`/`false_positive` issues can be scan-corroborated via `resolution_attestation.scan_verified` instead of being rewritten to `auto_resolved`. I also stopped scan-time stale holistic review expiry from auto-closing work in [issues.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/issues.py), and updated review-import completion so explicit imports mark covered review items `fixed` with `agent_import` attestation in [resolution.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/intelligence/review/importing/resolution.py) and [holistic_cache.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/intelligence/review/importing/holistic_cache.py).

I cleaned up the user-facing wording so the plan no longer implies “scan resolved this” in [cmd.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/cmd.py) and [render_sections.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/planning/render_sections.py), and documented the new rule in [QUEUE_LIFECYCLE.md](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/docs/QUEUE_LIFECYCLE.md).   Real. Prepare/run-batches drift risk is legitimate.
- `mid_level_elegance::triage_stage_order_contract_split`
  Real. Different stage lists controlling ordering is an actual correctness risk.
- `test_strategy::queue_command_paths_lack_integration_tests`
  Real. Those flows are still tested too seam-heavily.
- `type_safety::review_import_boundary_reverts_to_raw_dicts`
  Real. Especially now that I already unified part of the import loader path.

**Probably Worth Doing, But Larger / More Expensive**
These could help, but they are architectural and easier to make worse if done clumsily.

- `cross_module_architecture::language_framework_depends_upward_on_engine`
- `cross_module_architecture::state_facade_remains_codebase_hub`
- `incomplete_migration::state_compat_facade_remains_primary_runtime_api`
- `incomplete_migration::triage_epics_aliases_still_shape_runtime`
- `initialization_coupling::lazy_hook_lookup_bootstraps_language_modules`
- `low_level_elegance::post_scan_sync_kitchen_sink`
- `mid_level_elegance::private_dimension_prompt_handoff`
- `type_safety::language_runtime_contract_erased_to_any`

These are legitimate, but I would only do them if I can keep the change narrow and ownership-driven.

**Low Value / Likely To Make The Code Worse**
These are the ones I would lean toward `wontfix` or at least deprioritize heavily.

- `ai_generated_debt::runner_instruction_ceremony`
  Mostly UX tone/verbosity, not real code quality.
- `ai_generated_debt::triage_agent_nudge_boilerplate`
  Same. Could become churny “reduce wording” work.
- `convention_outlier::mixed_public_facade_protocols`
  Maybe true, but broad consistency cleanup across unrelated public surfaces is easy to overdo.
- `high_level_elegance::queue_and_triage_flow_has_no_single_home`
  Too abstract unless tied to a concrete ownership refactor.
- `high_level_elegance::top_level_package_taxonomy_blur`
  Likely repo taxonomy churn, not meaningful near-term improvement.
- `naming_quality::ambiguous_get_default_path`
  Low-value rename by itself.
- `naming_quality::generic_command_bucket_modules`
  Broad naming cleanup; easy to produce churn without real gain.
- `package_organization::base_root_config_straggler`
- `package_organization::framework_root_catchall`
- `package_organization::treesitter_root_keeps_compat_clutter`
- `package_organization::typescript_detectors_flat_bucket`
  These are mostly package reshuffles. High churn, unclear payoff.
- `test_strategy::smoke_tests_count_as_coverage_for_priority_modules`
  Directionally true, but unless tied to specific bad smoke-only tests, this becomes blanket testing philosophy churn.

**Questionable / Case-By-Case**
- `initialization_coupling::php_import_resolver_caches_lack_runtime_invalidation`
  Might be real, but only if those caches actually survive meaningfully across scan boundaries in production use.
- `low_level_elegance::batch_run_runtime_positional_bundle`
  Could help, but may just be style unless the call sites are truly error-prone.

So my honest cut is:
- `12` strong candidates worth doing
- `8` maybe-worth-doing architectural items
- `12` low-value items I would probably skip/wontfix
- `2` need a closer read

If you want the best path forward, I would continue in this order:
1. `error_consistency::plan_load_failure_contract_drift`
2. `mid_level_elegance::duplicated_review_packet_contract`
3. `mid_level_elegance::triage_stage_order_contract_split`
4. `abstraction_fitness::orchestrator_wrapper_chain`
5. `abstraction_fitness::typed_dict_plan_state_bag`

That order keeps the work concrete and reduces the risk of large churny refactors.

Yes. The root cause is now clear.

Why it said `mid-cycle scan`:
- [plan_reconcile.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/scan/plan_reconcile.py) classifies a scan as mid-cycle when:
  - `is_mid_cycle(plan)` is true, and
  - `queue_order` still has any non-skipped items
- In the saved plan, that was true:
  - `plan_start_scores` exists
  - `lifecycle_phase` is still `execute`
  - `queue_order_len = 39`
  - `non_skipped_queue_items = 39`

So the scan did not think we were at a fresh cycle boundary. It saw an active plan cycle with latent queued work, and intentionally preserved queue structure instead of regenerating clusters/triage.

That means the deviation was:
- visually, `next` had collapsed down to the `scan` step
- but structurally, the plan was not actually “empty and reset”
- so reconcile treated the scan as a refresh inside an active cycle, not a brand-new cycle start

> AGENT

Yes, I got to the bottom of it.

**What happened**
- The triage input was complete.
- The triage runner did not fully finish incorporation.
- The system kept partial stage state and partial manual recovery state instead of forcing a clean all-or-nothing result.

Concrete evidence:
- `collect_triage_input(...)` currently sees `46` open review issues.
- The `3` “missing” issues are definitely in that input:
  - `dependency_health::scan_workflow_cycle`
  - `logic_clarity::import_sync_ignores_deferred_scan_gate`
  - `test_strategy::queue_flow_integration_blind_spot`
- The current triage metadata is stale:
  - `epic_triage_meta.triaged_ids` still contains the old `22` issues from the previous completed triage
  - the new triage never reached completion, so that snapshot was never updated
- The plan shows partial recovery state:
  - `queue-lifecycle-hardening` exists
  - but it has `0` issue IDs and `0` action steps
- There are still exactly `3` open review issues unclustered

So the failure was not “the observe step never saw them.”
It was “the triage process was allowed to stop in a partially incorporated state.”

**Was everything visible in observe/reflect?**
Yes.

The observe/reflect prompt path uses the full `TriageInput.open_issues`, and that currently includes all of the missing IDs. So if by “the three-hour step” you mean the early triage analysis stage, then yes: those issues were visible there.

**Does triage know it can backlog or wontfix things?**
Yes, for `wontfix`.

The runner prompt explicitly teaches:
- `plan cluster create`
- `plan cluster add`
- `plan skip --permanent ... --note ... --attest ...`

So the intended model is:
- every open review issue must end up in a manual cluster
- or be permanently skipped/wontfixed

There is not really a separate “leave it floating in backlog unclustered” mode during triage. Completion policy explicitly rejects that.

**Where should the guarantee live?**
The hard guarantee should be at `triage complete`.

That is the right invariant:
- every open review issue in the triage snapshot must be exactly one of:
  - in a manual cluster
  - permanently skipped
  - explicitly dismissed by a triage-time disposition record

Right now completion already checks something close to that, but too weakly and too late in the recovery flow.

I would also keep a softer guarantee at `organize`:
- `organize` should not confirm if any open review issue lacks a cluster/skip disposition

That check already exists too. The problem is that partial manual recovery after stage execution can still leave the plan in an in-between state.

**So what is the actual bug?**
Not one bug, really two:

1. `run-stages` can leave behind confirmed-looking stage artifacts without a completed triage snapshot.
   - stage reports exist
   - but `triaged_ids` was never updated
   - so the plan looks half-done

2. Recovery after a failed completion is too loose.
   - you can create partial clusters like `queue-lifecycle-hardening` with no members
   - the system does not force a single explicit unresolved set and a single next repair action
   - that makes it easy for a few issues to remain unassigned while the queue still looks mostly normal

**How should it be enforced?**
Best enforcement model:

1. Freeze the required issue set at triage start.
   - store the exact review IDs being triaged, not just a hash

2. Require explicit disposition for every frozen ID before completion.
   - clustered
   - permanent skip
   - or explicit triage dismissal

3. Validate that at `organize`, `sense-check`, and `complete`.
   - `organize`: block early
   - `sense-check`: warn/fail if the set changed or if any IDs are unresolved
   - `complete`: hard fail with exact missing IDs

4. If `run-stages` fails completion, surface a dedicated recovery state.
   - not just `TRIAGE PENDING`
   - something like: “3 review issues still undispositioned”
   - and list the exact IDs

5. Disallow empty manual clusters from counting as progress.
   - `queue-lifecycle-hardening` should either not persist empty, or be flagged as invalid immediately

**How do we avoid this in the future?**
The key is to make triage disposition-driven, not artifact-driven.

That means:
- don’t infer success from “stage reports exist”
- don’t infer coverage from “some clusters were created”
- compute coverage from the frozen triage issue set every time

The missing invariant today is:
- “every triaged issue has an explicit disposition record”

Cluster membership alone is too indirect.

**Bottom line**
- The missing issues were not hidden.
- They were visible to triage.
- They were not fully dispositioned.
- The runner allowed a partial triage state to survive.
- The right hard guarantee is at `complete`, with the same coverage check already enforced earlier at `organize`.
- The fix is to freeze the triage issue set, require explicit per-issue disposition, and make failed completion leave a precise recovery state instead of vague pending mode.

If you want, I can turn this into a concrete implementation plan for the triage guarantee fix.

Yes. The pre-`organize` step is not definitive enough in the way that matters.

What I found:

- `reflect` is definitive for coverage.
  It enforces: every open review issue must appear exactly once in the `Coverage Ledger`.
- But `reflect` is not definitive for disposition.
  It does not persist a machine-readable “this issue must be skipped” vs “this issue must be clustered into X” contract.
- `organize` mostly treats the reflect blueprint as text guidance.
  The prompt tells the subagent to follow it, but validation does not check that the final plan mutations match the ledger.

That is the gap.

The concrete evidence is `review_batch_wrapper_chain`:
- the reflect/organize materials explicitly said:
  `review_batch_wrapper_chain -> skip "core-runner-already-collapsed"`
- but in the actual plan it still ended up in `triage-runner-simplification`
- `organize` still confirmed successfully

So the system currently guarantees:
- every issue is mentioned in reflect
- every issue is eventually covered by cluster or skip in organize

But it does **not** guarantee:
- the cluster/skip decision made in reflect is the one actually applied in organize

Why this slipped through:
- `_validate_reflect_issue_accounting(...)` only checks exact-once issue accounting
- `_validate_organize_stage(...)` checks:
  - no unclustered issues
  - clusters exist
  - clusters are enriched
  - cluster ops happened
  - report references cluster names
- it does **not** compare plan state against the reflect coverage ledger
- reflect stores only:
  - `cited_ids`
  - `missing_issue_ids`
  - `duplicate_issue_ids`
  - report text
- it does not store a structured per-issue disposition map

So yes: pre-`organize` is definitive enough for “nothing gets dropped,” but not definitive enough for “the blueprint is faithfully executed.”

What should be different:
- `reflect` should parse and persist a structured ledger:
  - `issue_id -> {"kind": "cluster", "target": "triage-runner-simplification"}`
  - `issue_id -> {"kind": "skip", "target": "core-runner-already-collapsed"}`
- `organize` should validate actual mutations against that persisted ledger
- if an issue that reflect said `skip` is still clustered, `organize` should fail
- if an issue that reflect said `cluster "X"` ends up skipped or in cluster `Y`, `organize` should fail unless the subagent explicitly re-records reflect

So the answer is:
- yes, the pre-organize stage is not definitive enough
- not because it failed to see issues
- but because it never became a machine-enforced execution contract for organize

- validation becomes deterministic

> AGENT

Yes. Looking through the actual triage flow, the pre-`organize` stage is not definitive enough.

What I found:

- `observe` is already fairly structured.
  It records per-issue `assessments` with:
  - `hash`
  - `verdict`
  - `verdict_reasoning`
  - `files_read`
  - `recommendation`

- `reflect` is only definitive for coverage, not execution.
  It validates:
  - every issue appears exactly once in the `Coverage Ledger`
  - skip lines have non-empty reasons
  But it does **not** persist a machine-readable “issue X must be permanently skipped” or “issue Y must go to cluster Z” ledger.

- `organize` is told to treat reflect as authoritative.
  The prompt literally says the reflect blueprint is authoritative and includes lines like:
  - `review_batch_wrapper_chain -> skip "core-runner-already-collapsed"`
  - `triage_pipeline_pass_throughs -> cluster "triage-runner-simplification"`

- But `organize` validation does not enforce that exact mapping.
  It checks:
  - no unclustered issues
  - clusters exist and are enriched
  - some cluster operations happened
  - the report mentions cluster names
  It does **not** check:
  - reflect said `skip`, but plan still clustered it
  - reflect said cluster `A`, but plan put it in cluster `B`

So the real answer is:

- the pre-`organize` stage is definitive enough for:
  - “nothing gets dropped”
  - “everything is covered”
- it is **not** definitive enough for:
  - “organize must reproduce the exact reflect disposition plan”

That is exactly why `review_batch_wrapper_chain` could:
- be marked `skip` in the reflect/organize materials
- but still remain clustered in actual plan state
- without `organize` failing

So yes, the weakness is real, and it is specifically the lack of a binding machine-readable reflect ledger between `reflect` and `organize`.
